prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Lange deutsche Komposita (language de).
Grid: 3 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Begriff" · longest unbreakable unit 546px · widest one-line content 546px
  col 2: header "Kurzform" · longest unbreakable unit 83px · widest one-line content 101px
  col 3: header "Erklärung" · longest unbreakable unit 186px · widest one-line content 1091px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 720px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 720px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 720px (column widths summing to more than 719px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 719px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Several designers worked independently on this table. You see their final layouts, anonymised as Layout P, Layout Q, Layout R, Layout S, Layout T, Layout U, in that order after the overview: Layout P, Layout Q (full view, then viewport view), Layout R (full view, then viewport view), Layout S, Layout T (full view, then viewport view), Layout U.
Measured facts:
Layout P: column widths [300, 122, 297] px · table 720×743 px · row heights [36, 129, 106, 129, 129, 83, 129] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 5 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 2 · fits the 720 px viewport (no scrolling)
Layout Q: column widths [300, 122, 350] px · table 773×604 px · row heights [36, 106, 83, 106, 106, 83, 83] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 4 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 2 · WIDER than the viewport by 53 px (horizontal scrolling)
Layout R: column widths [567, 122, 380] px · table 1070×580 px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 106, 106, 83, 83] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 4 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 350 px (horizontal scrolling)
Layout S: column widths [305, 122, 292] px · table 720×743 px · row heights [36, 129, 106, 129, 129, 83, 129] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 5 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 2 · fits the 720 px viewport (no scrolling)
Layout T: column widths [380, 122, 400] px · table 903×534 px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 106, 83, 60, 83] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 4 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 2 · WIDER than the viewport by 183 px (horizontal scrolling)
Layout U: column widths [310, 104, 305] px · table 720×720 px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 129, 129, 83, 129] · column headers on >1 line: 0/3 · tallest cell 5 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 2 · fits the 720 px viewport (no scrolling)

Compare them side by side. For each layout name its strengths, its faults and the spatial logic behind it (how it distributes space and why). Do not just pick a winner: you may combine the strengths of several layouts, propose something new, or overturn all of them. Propose up to 3 new designs that you expect to be better than every layout shown; if you believe one shown layout cannot be improved, say so in "best" and propose fewer or none.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"analysis":[{"layout":"name","strengths":"","faults":"","spatial_logic":""}],"insights":"what the comparison teaches about this table","best":["names of the best layout(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"idea":"what it combines or changes, and why"}]}
